title: Use basic horse tack, blankets and boots

lessons.title: Fitting basic tack: headcollar, saddle and bridle
lessons.html:
What is tack?

Tack is the equipment a horse wears to be handled and ridden. Basic tack is the headcollar, lead rope, saddle with girth and stirrups, and the bridle. Tack must fit well. Bad fit hurts the horse and can cause accidents.

The headcollar

A headcollar is used to lead and tie the horse. Fit: two fingers under the noseband, which sits a few centimetres below the cheekbone. Not so loose that a foot can get caught in it.

Parts of the saddle

  • Pommel - the front
  • Seat - where the rider sits
  • Cantle - the back
  • Flaps - the leather on each side
  • Stirrup leathers and stirrup irons - for the rider's feet
  • Girth - goes under the belly to hold the saddle on

Fitting the saddle

  1. Brush the back first.
  2. Put the saddle pad on a little forward, then the saddle on top.
  3. Slide both back so the saddle sits just behind the shoulder.
  4. Do up the girth slowly. Check it again before the rider gets on.
  5. The saddle must not touch the horse's spine. You should see light under the front arch.

Parts of the bridle

  • Headpiece - over the head behind the ears
  • Browband - across the forehead
  • Cheekpieces - down the sides, holding the bit
  • Noseband - around the nose
  • Throat lash - under the throat
  • Bit - in the mouth
  • Reins - for the rider's hands

Fitting the bridle

  1. Reins over the head first.
  2. Bit on your flat hand. Gently put it into the mouth.
  3. Headpiece over the ears, one at a time.
  4. Throat lash: a hand's width loose.
  5. Noseband: two fingers under it.
  6. The bit makes one or two small wrinkles at the corners of the mouth.

Always stand on the left side of the horse and keep your head out of the way if the horse throws its head.

lessons.title: Taking apart, cleaning and putting back tack
lessons.html:
Why clean tack?

Sweat, dirt and grease make leather hard and cracked. Hard leather rubs the horse and can break. Clean tack lasts longer and is safer. Wipe tack after every ride. Clean it fully once a week.

What you need

  • A bucket of warm water (not hot)
  • Two sponges: one to wash, one for saddle soap
  • Saddle soap
  • Leather oil or conditioner (used now and then, not every day)
  • A cloth and an old toothbrush
  • A saddle horse (stand) and a bridle hook

Taking the bridle apart

Hang the bridle on the hook. Undo each buckle and take off the parts one by one: reins, noseband, cheekpieces, bit. Lay them in order on a clean table. Remember the holes each buckle was on; you can note them or count them.

Cleaning

  1. Wash the bit in clean water and dry it. Never put soap on the bit.
  2. Wipe each piece of leather with the damp sponge to take off dirt and sweat. Use the toothbrush on stubborn spots.
  3. Rub saddle soap onto the second sponge (only a little damp) and work it into the leather, both sides.
  4. Clean the buckles and push soap out of the holes.
  5. Check for cracks, broken stitching and worn holes. Report them.

The saddle

Take off the stirrups, leathers and girth. Clean the seat, flaps and underside the same way. Wash the stirrup irons. Brush or wash the girth and saddle pad.

Putting it back together

Put each piece back on the same holes. Check that all straps go through their keepers. Hang the bridle neatly with the reins looped. Put the saddle on a saddle rack with the stirrups run up. Store tack in a dry, locked tack room.

lessons.title: Blankets and boots
lessons.html:
Horse blankets (rugs)

Blankets, also called rugs, keep a horse warm, dry or clean.

TypeUse
Stable rugWarmth in the stable on cold nights
Turnout rug (waterproof)In the camp in rain and cold
Fly sheetProtects from flies in summer
Cooler or sweat sheetHelps a hot, wet horse dry after work or a bath

Fitting a rug

  1. Fold the rug in half, front to back. Put it on gently over the withers, a little forward.
  2. Do up the front (chest) straps first.
  3. Unfold the rug over the back and slide it back so the hair lies flat.
  4. Do up the belly straps (surcingles), then leg straps if there are any.
  5. To take it off, undo leg straps and belly straps first, and front straps last.

A good fit: no rubbing on the shoulders or withers, the rug reaches the tail, you can fit a hand flat under the belly straps. Do not over-rug in warm weather; a sweating horse under a rug is too hot.

Caring for rugs

Check rugs every day for tears and broken straps. Brush off dirt. Wash and dry them as the label says. Store clean and dry, folded, away from rats.

Horse boots

BootUse
Brushing bootsProtect the lower legs from knocks by the other leg, during riding and lungeing
Overreach (bell) bootsProtect the heels of the front feet from the hind feet
Travel bootsProtect legs during transport

Fitting boots

  • Brush the legs clean first.
  • Put the boot a little high, then slide it down so the hair lies flat.
  • Straps on the outside of the leg, pointing backwards.
  • Do up the middle strap first, then the others. Not too tight: one finger under each strap.
  • Take boots off straight after work; check the legs for rubs.

Clean boots after use, brush out sand, and dry them before storing.

Key points

  • Saddle sits behind the shoulder and must not touch the spine.
  • Throat lash a hand's width; noseband two fingers.
  • Clean tack with saddle soap; never soap the bit; check for cracks.
  • Rug on: front straps first. Rug off: front straps last.
  • Boot straps on the outside, pointing back; one finger under each strap.
